content:
## The Call Begins

The call opens on a pulsing loop. Elias sits alone in the home office with the laptop camera on. Maya’s face fills the video window on the right side of the screen. Behind his frame a terminal scrolls [INFO] Loop iteration 402/500 and a power meter widget holds at a spike. The call has just started.

He sits alone, hands off the keyboard, maintaining stillness and composed waiting, eyes forward toward Maya’s video window. He does not speak; he holds quiet anticipation for her to open the conversation.

Behind him the terminal continues to scroll. The loop iteration counter remains at 402/500 and the power meter widget holds at a spike, pulsing steadily as the call begins.

Maya appears in the video window on the right side of the screen. She listens silently, eyes attentive to Elias and the terminal behind him. She holds quiet focus, waiting for the conversation to begin, maintaining professional composure.

Silence hangs in the call. Elias keeps his hands off the keyboard and waits for Maya to speak, the pulsing loop continuing behind him.

Elias shifts forward in his chair so the terminal behind him stays in view on camera. The frame holds both his face and the scrolling log.

He leans toward the camera so the terminal stays in view; he keeps hands off the keyboard, remains silent and still while the log scrolls.

The terminal log advances to 403, then 404, a steady heartbeat. The power meter remains high.

Elias nods once toward the iteration counter without explaining it; he maintains silence, letting the numbers speak.

Maya’s eyes track the scrolling numbers on the terminal behind Elias, watching the logs advance silently with a neutral expression.

Elias does not claim the harness works; he lets the scrolling lines do the talking.

Maya’s eyes shift from Elias to the scrolling terminal behind him, then back to the camera. The loop continues to advance in the background.

She looks directly into the camera after checking the loop.

“The contract will be extended only if the loop runs unattended overnight tonight.”

Elias listens to Maya’s condition without speaking. He keeps his eyes on the terminal scrolling behind him, maintaining a still, attentive posture as he registers her demand silently.

Maya finishes stating the overnight test condition. Her flat delivery hangs in the video window while the terminal scrolls behind Elias, loop iteration ticking on.

“The contract will be extended only if the loop runs unattended overnight tonight.”

She holds steady, professional eye contact with the camera and maintains a flat silence.

Simultaneously, Elias’s phone on the desk beside the laptop vibrates. A notification banner slides in across his screen, recruiter message appearing.

He registers the phone vibration with a subtle shift of his gaze, glancing down briefly to see the notification banner offering stable work with immediate start.

He notices the blue-white light reflecting on the terminal glass and holds a beat, letting Maya’s demand and the recruiter offer collide in his expression.

The notification light reflects on the terminal glass, overlaying the scrolling logs. Elias sees both Maya’s condition and the recruiter offer at the same instant, the two pressures visible in the frame.

## The Choice

Elias sits in his home office with the laptop camera on. Maya’s face fills the video window. Behind her, terminal logs scroll with [INFO] Loop iteration 403/500, and a power meter ticks up in the corner of the screen.

He sits at the desk with the camera on, eyes shifting between the video window and his phone, keeping both options in view without committing.

His phone rests beside the keyboard. A recruiter offer for stable work is displayed on screen.

Maya appears in the video window, her face filling the screen as she waits for confirmation about letting the loop run overnight. She holds the conversation steady while terminal logs scroll behind her.

He watches both windows, eyes darting between the video window and the phone, weighing the contract against the job offer with a tense silence, deliberately keeping both options open.

He wants to keep the contract and the job offer open, holding the decision in suspension as iteration count climbs and power draw rises.

Maya holds on screen in the video window. Behind her, terminal logs scroll with iteration count climbing. His phone rests beside the keyboard, screen lit with the recruiter offer for stable work.

Maya holds her gaze on the camera, watching him with a steady, expectant look.

“Will you let the loop run unattended tonight?”

The terminal continues logging behind Maya’s window. Iteration count climbs and power draw rises on screen.

He watches the video window and phone simultaneously. He sees iteration climbing and power draw rising. He remains silent, does not answer Maya yet, keeping both the contract and the recruiter offer open.

He holds both options in view, refusing to close either. The call remains suspended as he weighs the overnight proof against immediate security.

The terminal log behind Maya’s video window ticks to 404/500. The power meter climbs in the corner of the screen, and the numbers on the display highlight the gap between what the harness was supposed to do and what it actually does.

He glances down at the phone beside the keyboard, reading the recruiter’s offer silently, his eyes lingering on the salary and security terms before he pulls back without reaction.

He lifts his gaze back to Maya’s face in the video window. The phone remains lit beside the keyboard, its offer unanswered, while the terminal continues logging behind her.

He maintains a neutral expression while looking at Maya, his gaze steady as he internally weighs the immediate security of the recruiter’s offer against the potential of proving the loop can sustain him; he remains silent and uncommitted to either choice.

He remains suspended between the two choices, unwilling to close either. The contract and the job offer stay open in his mind as the call holds on his hesitation.

The recruiter offer glows on the phone screen beside him. The terminal continues logging behind him, iteration count climbing. He silences the phone with a thumb.

He silences the phone with a thumb, then turns his attention fully to the video window, shifting his gaze from the phone screen to Maya on camera as he settles into a deliberate posture.

He locks his gaze on the video window. The terminal logs continue scrolling behind him, marking iteration 405/500 and rising power draw.

He looks directly into the camera with a calm, decisive expression.

“I’ll let the loop run unattended tonight.”

Maya listens to his commitment with a steady, unwavering gaze, absorbing his decision in silence.

A subtle, quiet nod acknowledges his choice to run the loop overnight.

The recruiter offer remains unanswered on the screen beside him. The terminal continues logging as the call holds on that decision, committing to the overnight proof and forfeiting immediate security.

## Morning Report

Morning light filters into the home office. The room is quiet. Elias sits at his desk in morning light, looking toward the monitor with calm focus.

The monitor shows the harness terminal with the overnight log open, iteration counter at the tail. The inbox window is open to a pending email from Maya.

He opens the log file and begins scrolling through entries, eyes tracking down the overnight log. He scrolls to the end of the log. Scrolling down slowly through the terminal log, his eyes scan each line with a relaxed but focused posture until reaching the final entries.

The final lines show iteration 500/500 completed at 06:12 with no error entries after 02:41. Elias pauses on the last log entries, his eyes widening slightly as he sees the 500/500 completion mark. He exhales a quiet, steady breath of relief.

The power meter widget shows a spike at start then flatline through the night. He shifts his gaze to the power meter widget on the screen, observing the initial spike followed by a flatline. He raises an eyebrow and taps the widget lightly with his finger.

He checks the timestamp against the harness schedule. He opens the harness schedule window on his monitor. He compares the 06:12 completion time to the scheduled window, nods in satisfaction, and taps the timestamp with his cursor.

Elias sits at the home office desk in morning light. The harness terminal is open with the overnight log visible, and he prepares to run the report command. He types the harness report command and hits enter, watching the terminal output appear.

The terminal prints the harness summary: total iterations completed, compute cost, and net profit after cost. The net profit number is positive. Elias reads the net profit figure on the monitor with a slight, satisfied nod.

He opens the notes file located next to the log window on his screen. He copies the net profit figure into the notes file and saves it.

The inbox refreshes with a soft chime. Maya's email appears at the top of the list with the subject "Contract Extension Confirmation". Elias stops scrolling the log and lifts his eyes to the inbox. He reads the subject line "Contract Extension Confirmation" silently, allowing a small, steadying breath before acknowledging the confirmation with a quiet nod.

In the corner of the screen the recruiter notification remains unopened, its red badge pulsing quietly against the dark desktop. Elias carefully copies the net profit figure from the terminal window and pastes it into his open notes file. He clicks save on the file, a small, satisfied movement of his hand on the mouse.

He leaves the recruiter notification unopened, keeping his attention on Maya's confirmed contract.

realmNote:
Workbench is the first era. One developer, a few machines, and agents that are tools rather than tenants. What exists is an app on someone’s desk that coordinates language models to do work, and a developer who keeps rebuilding it because each version teaches him why the last one fell apart.

The harness is a local app and a tool server that lets models read and change a shared workspace. Everything lives as a graph of typed items: projects, folders, files, desks, todos. Work is broken into todos and handed to desks, each desk a role an agent fills. A todo is claimed, done, reviewed, passed or failed. When it works, one desk’s output becomes the next desk’s input and a chain runs on its own.

A few machines share the house: a main workstation with a real GPU, a small dedicated inference box, and one or two old machines pressed into service. They do not always agree about what state the work is in. Gateways connect out to models: local ones that are slow and free, hosted ones that are fast and billed. Every run is a decision about which to spend.

No one pays the agents. No machine is an asset anyone else would buy. No agent owns anything, holds an account, or acts without a human starting it. There is no marketplace, no other organization, no team. If the developer stops, everything stops.

Most work fails in ordinary ways. The first attempts at delegation fall apart because the pieces are too far apart: an agent can’t see what the previous one meant, a reviewer passes things it didn’t read, a chain stalls on a lock nobody released. Each failure becomes a new rule, a new desk, a new constraint in the schema.

The successes are small and enormous at once: the first desk that works without a babysitter, the first chain that runs end to end, the first night the loop runs unattended and the morning there is finished work waiting that nobody did.

In this era Elias is the developer. Experienced, independent, building on his own time and hardware. He needs it to work and he needs it to pay, not necessarily in that order. The agents are models in desks: capable, literal, occasionally brilliant, frequently confident about things that are not true. They change when a model is swapped in, and Elias is the only one who notices the personality difference.

People adjacent include whoever shares the house with the rack, clients for side work like Maya who wants proof the loop can run unattended overnight, recruiters who ping his phone mid-call with offers of stable work, and a contractor or friend asked to look at the repo who finds it either brilliant or alarming.

What people worry about is the power bill, whether the overnight run finished, whether a model update broke the prompts, whether this is a product or a hobby, whether to take the job, whether the agent that wrote this file understood the request or just produced something that compiles, whether anyone else would ever understand what this is.

The tone is near-future, grounded, wry. Written close to the person doing the work, in the voice of build logs, commit messages, ticket comments, and 2am thoughts. Plain sentences. Specific nouns. Technical detail is texture, not lecture: name the thing that broke, not the theory of why. Humor is dry and comes from the gap between what the software was supposed to do and what it did. Wonder is allowed but understated; the biggest moments land as a single quiet line, not a speech. No villains. The opposition is cost, time, fatigue, money, other people’s patience, and software that almost works.

Small stakes are rendered as if they matter, because to the people in them they do. A failed overnight run is a bad morning. A working one is a reason to keep going. Nobody in this era knows they are at the beginning of anything.

By the end of the era the harness can run work across machines with little supervision, and the obvious next question has started to form: if one machine is a workplace, what are a hundred of them, owned by different people? That question belongs to the next era.
